explanations.explanation: You nailed it! Moab is the neighbor country across the Salt Sea where this family heads to escape the famine (Ruth 1:1). It was a tough move, but when there is no bread on the counter, you go where the ovens are still running.
Not Egypt this time, friend. While plenty of people in the Bible packed their bags for Egypt when food got tight, Elimelech takes his family east to the land of Moab (Ruth 1:1).
No, they don't head to Edom. They set their sights on the land of Moab to live for a while because of that terrible famine (Ruth 1:1).
Perfect bake! Ruth is the one (Ruth 1:4). Little did Naomi know, this young Moabite woman was going to stick closer than a sticky glaze on a fresh cinnamon roll.
Not Rachel. Rachel was Jacob's wife back in Genesis, hundreds of years before this story starts. Naomi's sons married Orpah and Ruth (Ruth 1:4).
No, Dinah is from a much earlier story in Genesis. The two Moabite daughters-in-law here are Orpah and Ruth (Ruth 1:4).

That's the sad truth. After losing her husband, Naomi loses both of her boys, Mahlon and Chilion, leaving her with no husband and no children in a foreign land (Ruth 1:5). I think this one really hurts.

explanations.answer: Her house in Moab burns down
explanations.explanation: No, the text doesn't mention any fires or lost houses. The tragedy here is far more personal: both of her sons, Mahlon and Chilion, pass away (Ruth 1:5).

explanations.answer: She falls sick and loses her sight
explanations.explanation: No, Naomi doesn't lose her sight, but she suffers a massive heartbreak when both of her sons die after they had lived in Moab for about ten years (Ruth 1:5).
That's it! Naomi hears the great news that the famine back home is over because the LORD has visited His people and provided them with food (Ruth 1:6). Time to pack up!
Not a king, baker. This is still back in the days when the judges ruled, and what Naomi hears is that the LORD has provided food for His people back in Judah (Ruth 1:6).
No, victory is great, but when you are starving, you want dinner. Naomi hears that the LORD has provided food for His people, so she gets ready to leave Moab (Ruth 1:6).

explanations.answer: Go back to their mothers' homes
explanations.explanation: Baked just right! Naomi selflessly tells them to go back where they have a family to look after them, saying, "Go back, each of you to your mother’s home" (Ruth 1:8).

explanations.answer: Walk faster to beat the dark
explanations.explanation: No, Naomi isn't trying to rush them down the road. She is actually trying to send them back home to Moab where they will be safe and comfortable (Ruth 1:8).

explanations.answer: Stay close to her the whole way
explanations.explanation: Actually, it's the opposite! Instead of telling them to stick close, Naomi tells them to go back to their own mothers' homes in Moab (Ruth 1:8).

You got it! Naomi blesses them and says, "May the LORD enable each of you to find rest in the home of your new husband" (Ruth 1:9). She wants them to have a future, even if it means leaving her behind.
It's actually True, friend. Naomi prays that the LORD will help each of them find rest in the home of a new husband back in Moab (Ruth 1:9).

explanations.answer: We will return with you to your people
explanations.explanation: Box-worthy! They both weep and say, "Surely we will return with you to your people" (Ruth 1:10). They loved her too much to let her make that long walk alone.

explanations.answer: We will stay in Moab and wait for you
explanations.explanation: No, they don't want to stay behind and wait. They both tell her right away, "Surely we will return with you to your people" (Ruth 1:10).

explanations.answer: We will come visit you in Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: No, they weren't planning a short vacation. They were ready to move for good, telling Naomi they would return with her to her people (Ruth 1:10).

explanations.answer: Would you wait for them to grow up
explanations.explanation: Exactly! Naomi is being highly practical here. She asks if they would really put their lives on hold and wait for imaginary future sons of hers to grow up to marry them (Ruth 1:11–13).

explanations.answer: Would you raise them as your own
explanations.explanation: Not quite. Naomi is asking about them finding husbands, asking if they would really wait around for her future sons to grow up to be married (Ruth 1:13).

explanations.answer: Would you go ahead to Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: No, Naomi is trying to convince them to go back to Moab. She asks them if they would wait around for any future sons she might have to grow up (Ruth 1:13).

explanations.answer: The LORD's hand has turned against her
explanations.explanation: Perfect! Naomi is carrying a heavy load of grief, and she believes "the hand of the LORD has gone out against me" (Ruth 1:13). She feels like she is under a dark cloud.

explanations.answer: The people of Judah have turned against her
explanations.explanation: No, Naomi doesn't say anything about the people back in Judah. Her grief is deeper than that: she feels that the hand of the LORD has gone out against her (Ruth 1:13).

explanations.answer: The people of Moab have turned against her
explanations.explanation: No, the Moabites aren't the issue here. Naomi tells her daughters-in-law that her life is bitter because she feels the hand of the LORD has gone out against her (Ruth 1:13).
Spot on! Orpah decides to take Naomi's advice. She kisses her mother-in-law goodbye and heads back to her family (Ruth 1:14).
Actually, it's True, baker. Orpah kisses Naomi goodbye and turns back, while Ruth is the one who clings to her (Ruth 1:14).
No, that's underbaked. While Orpah goes back, Ruth does the exact opposite. The text says Orpah kissed her goodbye, "but Ruth clung to her" (Ruth 1:14). Ruth isn't going anywhere.
That's a keeper! It is False because Ruth refuses to leave. While Orpah heads back to Moab, Ruth clings tightly to Naomi (Ruth 1:14).
Baked just right! Naomi points to Orpah's departure and urges Ruth, "follow her back home" (Ruth 1:15). She is giving Ruth one last exit ramp.
It's actually True. Even after Ruth refuses the first time, Naomi sees Orpah walking away and tells Ruth, "follow her back home" (Ruth 1:15).

explanations.answer: Naomi's God will be her God
explanations.explanation: That's it! This is a massive moment. Ruth isn't just changing her address; she is choosing the LORD, promising, "your people will be my people, and your God will be my God" (Ruth 1:16).

explanations.answer: She will take care of Naomi's house
explanations.explanation: No, Ruth promises something much deeper than doing chores. She vows that Naomi's people will be her people, and Naomi's God will be her God (Ruth 1:16).

explanations.answer: She will learn all the ways of Judah
explanations.explanation: No, Ruth's promise goes way beyond learning customs. She commits her heart, saying, "your people will be my people, and your God will be my God" (Ruth 1:16).
Perfect bake! Ruth seals her promise with a solemn vow: "May the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, if anything but death separates you and me" (Ruth 1:17). That is absolute loyalty.
No, distance isn't going to stop Ruth. She goes all the way, swearing that nothing but death itself will separate them (Ruth 1:17).
No, Ruth isn't worried about marriage separating them. She makes a vow that only death will ever keep her and Naomi apart (Ruth 1:17).

explanations.answer: She stops trying to persuade her
explanations.explanation: You got it! When Naomi sees that Ruth is completely set on going with her, she realizes there is no changing her mind, so she stops trying to persuade her (Ruth 1:18).

explanations.answer: She sends her back after Orpah
explanations.explanation: No, Naomi has already tried that multiple times. Once she sees how determined Ruth is, she stops trying to talk her out of it (Ruth 1:18).

explanations.answer: She tells her to wait in Moab
explanations.explanation: No, they are already on the road. When Naomi sees Ruth's determination, she drops the arguments and lets her come along (Ruth 1:18).
Box-worthy! The whole town is buzzing when they see her, exclaiming, "Can this be Naomi?" (Ruth 1:19). Ten years and a lot of grief can change a person's look, friend.
No, they don't ask about her husband. They are just shocked to see her back, asking each other, "Can this be Naomi?" (Ruth 1:19).
No, they recognize Naomi, even if she looks different. The women of the town whisper and ask, "Can this be Naomi?" (Ruth 1:19).
Perfect! Naomi means "pleasant," but she says, "Do not call me Naomi... Call me Mara," which means bitter, because of all the hardship she has faced (Ruth 1:20).
Not Hannah. Hannah is Samuel's mother in a different story. Naomi tells them to call her Mara because she feels the Almighty has dealt bitterly with her (Ruth 1:20).
No, Leah was one of Jacob's wives in Genesis. Naomi wants to be called Mara to match the bitterness of her losses (Ruth 1:20).
No, that's underbaked. Naomi says the exact opposite! She tells them, "I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty" (Ruth 1:21). Her hands feel completely empty after losing her family.
That's a keeper! It is False because Naomi's words are, "I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty" (Ruth 1:21). She is mourning her husband and her sons.
Perfect bake! They roll into Bethlehem just as the barley harvest is getting started (Ruth 1:22). And friend, in a story about survival, a fresh harvest is a very good sign.
Not wheat, though that comes later in the season. Naomi and Ruth arrive right at the very beginning of the barley harvest (Ruth 1:22).
No, they don't arrive for the olives. The text tells us they reach Bethlehem at the start of the barley harvest (Ruth 1:22).
